evidence.says: Susan E. James, author of The Feminine Dynamic in English Art and Kateryn Parr, received a PhD from Cambridge University.
Back to the Source names Susan James at Pacifica Graduate Institute and gives ORCID 0000-0002-1224-3830.
Pacifica faculty member Susan James earned a PhD in Community Psychology from New York University.

basis: The works are associated with scholars whose reported doctorates and careers differ: a Cambridge-trained historian and an NYU-trained community psychologist. The article identifies the latter by the ORCID on key b.

evidence.says: Lists Margaret Hall as an author of Confronting Leviathan, published by Ohio University Press in 1997.
Cites Margaret Hall's A History of Women Faculty at the University of Washington, 1896–1970 as a 1984 University of Washington PhD dissertation.

basis: The sources identify the two works but do not establish that their authors are the same person or different people. The shared name alone is insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: Oikonomia urbana names Emanuele Camillo Colombo (1975) at Università Cattolica and lists his Giochi di luoghi.
Emanuele Camillo Colombo is a professor of economic history at Università Cattolica; his ORCID is 0000-0002-9280-9223.
Emanuele J Colombo is a Boston College professor and lists Enslaved Muslims on the Early Modern Italian Peninsula (2024).

basis: The publisher identifies the author of both books as Emanuele Camillo Colombo, whose university profile shows a continuing economic history career and a different ORCID. The author of the 2024 article has a distinct concurrent career at Boston College.

evidence.says: David G. Hunter holds the Catholic Studies chair at Kentucky and wrote Marriage, Celibacy, and Heresy in Ancient Christianity.
David Hunter was music librarian and senior lecturer at UT Austin from 1988 to 2017; he earned a PhD at Illinois and wrote The Lives of George Frideric Handel.

basis: The review credit identifies its David Hunter with UT Austin, where a music librarian held a long career overlapping the Kentucky career of the author of the other key's book. These distinct concurrent careers support two people; the association of the review credit with the librarian is inferred from the institutional affiliation.

evidence.says: Warren B. Smith selected White Servitude in Colonial South Carolina as a doctoral thesis subject in 1911; the book appeared in 1961.
Warren William Smith wrote The Rise of Sŏwŏn as a University of California doctoral dissertation, dated 1972.

basis: The dissertation is attributed to Warren William Smith, while the White Servitude author is Warren B. Smith, who had already selected his doctoral subject in 1911. Their names and doctoral timelines indicate different scholars; the source dates the Korean dissertation 1972 rather than the record's 1971.

evidence.says: Lists David Alan Wolff, “The Western coal industry in the era of expansion, 1868 to 1913,” in Dissertation Abstracts International, 2000.
David A. Wolff received a Ph.D. from Arizona State University and wrote Industrializing the Rockies.
David Wolff earned a history Ph.D. at UC Berkeley in 1991 and wrote To the Harbin Station.

basis: The coal dissertation is attributed to David Alan Wolff, consistent with the Arizona State doctorate and coal-history career of David A. Wolff. The Harbin author has a separate Berkeley doctorate and career; the identification of the coal dissertation author with the Arizona State graduate is inferred.

evidence.says: Jason Morgan Ward lists a Duke A.B. in 2001 and a Yale Ph.D. in 2008 with the dissertation Saving Segregation.

basis: The graph identifies the author of Unpacking the Mule as completing a doctoral dissertation in 2001, while Jason Morgan Ward's CV places his undergraduate degree in that year and his doctorate at Yale in 2008. These distinct degree timelines strongly indicate two scholars.

evidence.says: Northampton lists Matthew S. Seligmann's commentary at the 2009 conference and his books Spies in Uniform and Naval Intelligence from Germany.

basis: Northampton links the scholar on side b to the conference, but its record identifies a presentation rather than the conference review attributed to side a. The review attribution could not be independently verified, so this does not establish that the keys represent the same person.

evidence.says: Mel Piehl reviewed Earnestly Contending for H-Catholic in November 2014; no affiliation is given.
Mel Piehl, professor of history and humanities at Christ College, Valparaiso University, reviewed The View from Rome for H-Catholic in 2003.

basis: The two reviews share a reviewer name and publication venue, but the 2014 review gives no affiliation or other identifier tying its author to the 2003 reviewer. The available evidence does not establish that they are the same person.

evidence.says: Anna Suranyi earned a UCLA history PhD and wrote The Genius of the English Nation and The Atlantic Connection.
Northeastern lists history professor Anna Suranyi with a 2001 UCLA PhD.

basis: The book author's 2001 doctorate matches the thesis year, but the available evidence does not connect her to the named dissertation or establish its university. A shared name and subject do not establish identity.

evidence.says: The 2007 issue lists Peter Carrier's review of Mechtild Gilzmer's Denkmäler als Medien der Erinnerungskultur in Frankreich seit 1944.
Peter Carrier authored Holocaust Monuments and National Memory Cultures in France and Germany Since 1989, published in 2005.

basis: The sources identify the reviewer and book author by name but do not establish a connection between their works or careers. Their shared subject alone is insufficient to establish identity.

evidence.says: Cites Charles B. Forcey's review of Michael Schudson's The Power of News in H-Review, September 1997.
Charles Budd Forcey wrote The Crossroads of Liberalism, taught at Columbia before joining Binghamton in 1967, and retired in 1991.

basis: The author of the book taught at Columbia, but the source places him there before 1967, not at the time of the 1997 review. No source found ties the review to the book author.

evidence.says: Christine Keiner, a professor at Rochester Institute of Technology, is the author of The Oyster Question.

basis: The publisher identifies the author of the book on side b, but the accessible evidence does not independently connect her to the review on side a. The shared name alone is insufficient to establish identity.

evidence.says: UC Berkeley lists Ruth Marie Leacock's 1959 dissertation on Jacques Malet-DuPan.
Google Books credits Ruth Leacock with Requiem for Revolution, published in 1990.

basis: The sources identify the dissertation and book authors, but do not establish a connection between them. The shared name and compatible dates alone do not resolve the identity.

evidence.says: Damien Boquet obtained an habilitation in 2019; his listed works include Medieval Sensibilities and Politiques des émotions au Moyen Âge.

basis: The institutional page lists a 2019 habilitation and works from side a, but gives a different habilitation title and does not identify the synthesis memoir on side b. The matching name, year and subject alone do not establish the link.

evidence.says: David Saunders taught at Newcastle from 1979 to 2017 and lists The Ukrainian Impact on Russian Culture (1985).
The author of Wired-up in White Organdie is David Saunders, a PhD student at Queen Mary University of London in 2018.
David Saunders at Queen Mary University of London received a doctoral studentship in 2016.

basis: The author of the 1985 book was a long-serving Newcastle historian, while the author of the 2018 article held a doctoral studentship at Queen Mary during the same period. These contemporaneous careers indicate two different scholars.

evidence.says: The catalogue attributes White servitude in colonial South Carolina (1961) to Warren B. Smith.
The Alabama Review lists Warren I. Smith as author of Land Patterns in Ante-Bellum Montgomery County, Alabama (1955).

basis: No source found connects the 1952 dissertation author to the author of the 1961 book. The similarly titled 1955 article has a different middle initial, but its relationship to the dissertation is unconfirmed.

evidence.says: Lists Alan Wilbert Currie Green's Legacy of Illusion as a 1968 dissertation at the Claremont Colleges.
Lists Immigrants in the City by Alan Green as a 1973 Queen's University economics working paper.

basis: The dissertation bibliography gives the author a different set of middle names from the Alan G. Green label on the other key. The sources found do not establish either a shared identity or sufficiently distinct careers to settle the pair.

evidence.says: Kay Ann Johnson wrote China's Hidden Children and Wanting a Daughter, Needing a Son and was a professor at Hampshire College.
Kay Ann Johnson received a political science PhD from Wisconsin; her 1976 doctoral thesis concerned women and family reform in China.

basis: The reported 1976 doctoral thesis differs from the 1974 thesis assigned to the second key, but I could not independently verify the latter's degree or author. No source connects the two works or conclusively establishes two people.

evidence.says: A 1947 article cites John L. Harr, The Ante-Bellum Southwest, 1815-1861, University of Chicago, 1941.
The library catalog credits The Rockefeller Century (1988) to John Ensor Harr, born 1926, and Peter J. Johnson.

basis: The thesis is attributed to John L. Harr in 1941, when John Ensor Harr would have been about 15, and the middle initials differ. Together these strongly indicate different people, though the conclusion is inferred rather than explicitly stated by a source.

evidence.says: Juan González's CV lists Harvest of Empire, Fallout, News for All the People and Roll Down Your Window, and a Brooklyn College appointment in 2001–2003.
The 2016 article Río Grande, Bravo... y sangriento names Juan Ignacio Guijarro González, ORCID 0000-0001-7384-6515, Universidad de Sevilla.
In 2002, Universidad de Sevilla appointed Dr. Juan Ignacio Guijarro González professor of English philology.

basis: The book author and the article author have distinct overlapping careers: a New York journalist and Brooklyn College professor, and a Universidad de Sevilla professor of English philology. The article identifies the latter by the ORCID attached to b.

evidence.says: The bibliography attributes Massachusetts Anti-imperialism, 1895-1904 (1971) to Daniel Boone Schirmer.
Brown University Library identifies Daniel Boone Schirmer as the author of Republic or Empire (1972).
An obituary links Schirmer's doctoral dissertation on the Anti-Imperialist League and the Philippine-American War with his book Republic or Empire.

basis: The full name and the obituary's description of the doctoral subject strongly suggest a match, but the obituary does not identify the dissertation by title or university. No source found explicitly links the specific dissertation to the book or establishes that the book grew out of it.

evidence.says: Lists William L. Blackwell, Alexander I and Poland, as a Princeton PhD dissertation, 1959.
Lists William L. Blackwell as author of The Beginnings of Russian Industrialization, published in 1968.

basis: The sources attribute the dissertation and book to William L. Blackwell, but do not establish that the authors are the same person. The dissertation year is given as 1959 in the bibliography, versus 1960 in the supplied record.

evidence.says: Lists Lisa Dorr as the H-Law reviewer of Cheryl Hicks's Talk with You Like a Woman in April 2012.
Lisa Lindquist Dorr is an Alabama professor and author of White Women, Rape, and the Power of Race in Virginia, 1900-1960.

basis: The review listing does not identify its author's affiliation or another work, so the sources do not establish a link to Lisa Lindquist Dorr's career. The shared name and subject alone are insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: María del Socorro Morales de Casas authored Persistencia de las formas de vida campesina and was affiliated with IPN CIIDIR Durango.
UNLV history professor Maria Raquel Casas authored Married to a Daughter of the Land.
The 2021 UNLV directory lists Maria Casas as an associate professor in the History Department.

basis: The agricultural researcher at IPN Durango and the UNLV historian María Raquel Casas had distinct concurrent careers in 2021. The UNLV profile identifies the historian as the author of the book on side b.

evidence.says: Robert L. Frost of Wabash College wrote the PhD dissertation Alternating Currents: Technocratic Power and Workers' Resistance at Electricité de France, 1946-1970.
Robert Frost completed a Nottingham PhD on Wilkinson and lists A Forgotten Chapter in Egyptology and A Geologist and an Egyptologist in Conversation.
Robert Frost submitted Sir John Gardner Wilkinson: Lost Worlds of Antiquarianism in Egypt and the Balkans for a Nottingham PhD in 2022.

basis: The records point to different doctorates and careers: Robert L. Frost's electricity history PhD and the Leicester scholar's 2022 Nottingham PhD on Wilkinson. The latter's faculty page lists the works on side b.

evidence.says: M.A. Samuel Weber of the University of Bern's history institute wrote the 2014 report on Europäische Kongressorte der Frühen Neuzeit.
Christian Windler lists Samuel Weber's Aristocratic Power in the Spanish Monarchy among dissertations he supervised.
The Swiss National Library lists Samuel Weber, born 1987, as author of Aristocratic Power, a 2021 University of Bern dissertation.
Samuel Weber, born 1940, earned a Cornell doctorate in comparative literature in 1971 and wrote Benjamin's -abilities.

basis: The report is credited to a Bern historian whose career and Bern dissertation align with the Samuel Weber born in 1987. The author of Benjamin's -abilities was born in 1940 and earned a different doctorate in 1971.

evidence.says: Johns Hopkins University Press identifies Elizabeth Haiken as the author of Venus Envy: A History of Cosmetic Surgery.

basis: The publisher identifies the author of the book, but the sources found do not establish that the book author wrote the 1994 dissertation or that the book grew out of it. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: The 1989 University of Texas System docket lists George N. Green as a history professor at the University of Texas at Arlington.

basis: The institutional record supports the Arlington affiliation on side a, but no source found ties the side b review or its reviewer to that scholar. The shared name and subject are insufficient to establish identity.

evidence.says: James Neal Primm wrote Lion of the Valley and Economic Policy in the Development of a Western State and received a doctorate from the University of Missouri-Columbia.

basis: The source connects the author of Lion of the Valley to a doctorate and a book on Missouri economic policy, but does not identify the 1951 dissertation on the other key or establish that the book grew from it. The overlap in subject and name alone is insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: William & Mary lists In Babel's Shadow among Tuska Benes's books.
The 2004 AHA program lists Tuska Benes of the University of Pennsylvania as a conference presenter.

basis: The conference program places a Tuska Benes at the reviewer's institution in 2004, but the sources found do not establish that she is the author of In Babel's Shadow. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: M.A. Samuel Weber of the University of Bern coauthored the 2014 report on Protegierte und Protektoren.
Samuel Weber of the University of Bern studied history at Bern and earned a joint Bern–Durham doctorate in 2019.
Northwestern professor Samuel Weber wrote Benjamin's -abilities and Theatricality as Medium and previously taught at UCLA.

basis: The conference report is credited to a Bern historian whose subsequent academic career includes a 2019 doctorate. The author of the works on the other key had an established UCLA and Northwestern career and published those books years earlier, indicating two different scholars.

evidence.says: Beverly Boutilier co-edited Creating Historical Memory with Alison Prentice in 1997.
Beverly L. Boutilier wrote Gender, Organized Women, and the Politics of Institution Building, a Carleton University history PhD thesis dated 1993.

basis: The sources identify the editor and the dissertation author but do not establish a connection between them. The thesis citation gives 1993, while the graph lists 1994.

evidence.says: The LC authority identifies Timothy P. Maga with America, France, and the European refugee problem, 1933-1947 (1985).
McGill's thesis index lists Timothy P. Maga's The United States, France, and the refugee problem, 1933-1947 (1981).
The 2004–05 faculty catalogue lists Timothy P. Maga, history professor, with a PhD from McGill University.

basis: The thesis and book have closely corresponding titles, and a historian of the same name held a McGill PhD. The sources found do not explicitly link the book author to that degree or state that the book developed from the thesis.

evidence.says: Karen Smith, The Magnificent Experiment, Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara, 1982.
Karen Manners Smith, Marion Harland: The Making of a Household Word, Ph.D. dissertation, University of Massachusetts, 1990.

basis: The two works are separate history Ph.D. dissertations at different universities eight years apart. These distinct doctorates support treating the authors as different people.

evidence.says: David W. Beck completed the dissertation “Public Works in Spain, 1926-1933” at the University of New Mexico in 1980.
David R. M. Beck received a 1994 PhD at the University of Illinois Chicago for “Siege and Survival: Menominee Responses To An Encroaching World”.

basis: The two dissertation records identify David W. Beck and David R. M. Beck, with distinct history doctorates at different universities and dates. Their differing middle initials and doctoral records support treating them as different scholars.

evidence.says: In 2002 Michael D. Innis-Jiménez was a history graduate student at the University of Iowa.
Michael Innis-Jiménez earned a history Ph.D. at the University of Iowa and authored Steel Barrio.

basis: The sources connect Michael D. Innis-Jiménez at Iowa with the career of the author of Steel Barrio, but do not identify the author of the 1999 review by an independent career detail or link that review to the book author.

evidence.says: Christine R. Johnson reviewed Hans Staden's True History for H-German in May 2011; no affiliation is given.
Washington University history professor Christine Johnson wrote The German Discovery of the World (2008).

basis: The review and faculty page do not establish a link between the review and the book or place the reviewer at the same institution. The shared name and field alone are insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: Max M. Mintz authored Gouverneur Morris and the American Revolution and was professor emeritus of history at Southern Connecticut State University.

basis: The book and dissertation concern the same historical figure, but no source found connects the dissertation to the book or independently identifies their authors as the same person.

evidence.says: Elizabeth Barnes, author of States of Sympathy (1997), is an associate professor of English at the College of William and Mary.
Elizabeth Barnes, author of the article on freedmen and gendered authority, is a lecturer and recent PhD graduate at the University of Reading.
Liz Barnes describes her education at Queen Mary, UCL and Reading, and says she completed her PhD viva in 2020.

basis: The book author and the recent article author have distinct career histories: one was a William and Mary English professor, while the other completed a Reading doctorate in 2020. The 1999 review attached to b may belong to a different author and needs separate checking.

evidence.says: Debra A. Reid reviewed The Big House after Slavery for H-SAWH in October 2011; no affiliation is given.
Eastern Illinois University history faculty member Debra A. Reid published Reaping a Greater Harvest in 2007.

basis: The review does not identify its author's affiliation, and no source found connects that review to the author of Reaping a Greater Harvest. The matching name alone does not establish identity.

evidence.says: Michael W. Jennings lists Dialectical Images, a 1989 Virginia PhD in German literature, and Princeton German appointments from 1981 onward.
Michael Jennings of SOAS lists an Oxford BA in 1990–93, a SOAS PhD in African history in 1995–98, and SOAS employment from 2007.
SOAS identifies Michael Jennings as a professor of global development with a PhD from London and degrees from Oxford and SOAS.

basis: The SOAS review credit matches the SOAS scholar, whose education and career differ from those of the Princeton author of Dialectical Images. Their undergraduate and doctoral timelines identify two distinct careers.

evidence.says: Alan Davidson wrote The Oxford Companion to Food and North Atlantic Seafood; after diplomatic service he pursued a career as a food historian and writer.
Alan Davidson of the University of Connecticut Department of Sociology reviewed A Modern Heretic and a Traditional Community for H-AmRel in January 1999.

basis: The food writer's documented diplomatic and food-writing career differs from the Connecticut sociology affiliation and unrelated scholarly review in the same period. This is a strong inference from the distinct careers, rather than an explicit statement that they are different people.

evidence.says: The author note identifies Jonathan W. White with Christopher Newport University and lists A Philadelphia Perspective and Abraham Lincoln and Treason in the Civil War.

basis: The author note identifies works and an affiliation on side b, but I found no accessible source tying the side a review to that scholar. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Mark Tebeau is an Arizona State University historian and author of Eating Smoke; he holds a Ph.D. from Carnegie Mellon University.

basis: The ASU profile identifies the author of the book on side b, but the sources found do not connect him to the 1998 review or its Harvard Medical School affiliation. The shared name alone does not establish identity.

evidence.says: William McFerrin Stowe, Jr. wrote Willie Rainach and the defense of segregation in Louisiana, 1954-1959, a Texas Christian University dissertation, 1989.
William W. Stowe, Wesleyan professor of English emeritus, wrote Balzac, James, and the Realistic Novel (1983) and Going Abroad (1994).

basis: The dissertation is attributed to William McFerrin Stowe, Jr., while the books are attributed to William W. Stowe, a Wesleyan English professor. Their different middle initials and distinct scholarly careers during overlapping years indicate two people.
